title: Out-of-equilibrium finite-time percolation transitions and spinodal-like behaviors after quenches across magnetic first-order transitions of Ising systems
authors: Andrea Pelissetto, Davide Rossini, Ettore Vicari
abstract: We analyze the out-of-equilibrium relaxational dynamics of ferromagnetic Ising-like systems driven across their low-temperature magnetic first-order transition (FOT) line, by sudden and slow variations of an external homogenous magnetic field $h$. As a paradigmatic example, we consider a two-dimensional Ising system driven across its low-temperature FOT line by suddently quenching $h$ from $h_i<0$ to $h>0$, inducing a transition from the negatively to the positively magnetized phase. We show the emergence of a dynamic percolation transition at a finite critical time $t_c(h)$ along the post-quench evolution for finite (sufficiently small) values of $h$, which is marked by the percolation of the largest positive-spin cluster and the antipercolation of the largest negative-spin cluster. This out-of-equilibrium percolation transition displays a finite-size scaling behavior as in the standard random-percolation case. However, while the fractal dimension of the percolating clusters is consistent with the random-percolation value, the exponent controlling the approach to criticality differs and depends on $h$. We also show that the percolation transition marks the passage from the metastable negatively-magnetized phase to the stable positively-magnetized one. Therefore, in the small-$h$ limit, the percolation critical behavior is related to the spinodal-like behavior of the magnetization, implying that the percolation time $t_c(h)$ exhibits a spinodal-like exponential dependence on $h$. The existence of percolation transitions is likely a generic phenomenon at magnetic Ising-like FOTs. For example, we observe an analogous behavior in dynamic (Kibble-Zurek-like) protocols entailing slow variations of the magnetic field driving the crossing of the FOT line.
summary: This work investigates how Ising systems behave when rapidly quenched across a first-order magnetic phase transition. The authors find that the system undergoes a dynamic percolation transition at a finite time $t_c(h)$. This percolation event is shown to be intimately linked to the spinodal instability of the magnetization, suggesting a general mechanism for non-equilibrium transitions in such systems.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the out-of-equilibrium relaxational dynamics of ferromagnetic Ising-like systems driven across their low-temperature magnetic first-order transition (FOT) line.
main_result: It shows the emergence of a dynamic percolation transition at a finite critical time $t_c(h)$, which relates the percolation critical behavior to the spinodal-like exponential dependence of the magnetization in the small-$h$ limit.
method: The study uses Monte Carlo simulations to track the time evolution of spin clusters and analyze finite-size scaling behavior across the quench.
model_or_system: The model is a two-dimensional Ising system on a square lattice governed by a Hamiltonian including an external magnetic field $h$. The dynamics are studied using relaxational Monte Carlo simulations.
key_observables: Magnetization $M(t)$, the size of the largest positive and negative spin clusters ($\Sigma_{\pm}(t)$), and the critical time $t_c(h)$.
important_parameters: The external magnetic field $h$, the quench protocol (sudden vs. slow variation), and the system size $L$.
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on the large-volume limit ($V 	o \infty$) and assumes the dynamics are governed by relaxational processes.
figures_summary: The notes mention figures showing the time evolution of cluster sizes ($\Sigma_+(t)$ and $\Sigma_-(t)$) and the scaling behavior of these observables near the transition time $t_c$.
paper_structure: The paper analyzes the dynamics by first setting up the model and quench protocol, then identifying the percolation transition via cluster analysis, and finally relating the critical time scaling to the spinodal behavior of the magnetization.
why_interesting: The connection drawn between dynamic percolation and spinodal decomposition in the context of first-order phase transitions is a powerful tool for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in many-body systems, relevant for quench dynamics in quantum simulation.
